title: Circuit Design: An inquiry lab activity at Maui Community College
extended_summary:
This paper describes the design and classroom implementation of an inquiry-based circuit design lab for first-year community college students in Electrical Engineering Technology. The authors focus on how to adapt a science-inquiry format to an engineering-oriented inquiry activity, using the Wheatstone bridge as the central system for students to explore voltage dividers, Kirchhoff’s voltage law, and resistive network analysis.

The intervention was a hands-on lab in which students first completed “Starters” that exposed them to balanced and unbalanced bridge circuits, thermistors, and variable resistors. Students then generated questions that facilitators sorted into four engineering design goals: building a perfectly balanced bridge, building a bridge that operates in a linear regime, using the bridge as a thermometer, or using it to determine an unknown resistance. Teams selected one challenge, built and tested their own circuits from scratch on breadboards, and concluded by presenting posters and being assessed with a rubric designed for engineering inquiry.

The activity was implemented in Electronics 101 at Maui Community College with twelve primarily first-year undergraduate students. The paper’s main contribution is not an effect evaluation but a description of inquiry design elements, facilitation, and assessment changes needed when shifting from science inquiry to engineering inquiry. The authors conclude that the approach supported learning goals and student engagement, while also noting that the rubric needed improvement for reliability.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a descriptive conference paper about the design and implementation of an inquiry lab, not a controlled evaluation. It includes student work and rubric scores but no comparison group, randomization, or pre/post causal analysis.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests modest benefits for engineering process skills and engagement in a small class, but the evidence is qualitative and lacks effect sizes or a rigorous evaluation design. Any impact is therefore unclear and likely modest.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports an inquiry lab in circuit design with 12 first-year Electrical Engineering Technology students, focused on building and analyzing Wheatstone bridge circuits to meet engineering design goals. Students completed the activity and produced poster presentations, but the summative rubric showed only moderate performance (mean class score 6.2/9) and limited scoring reliability (mean SD=1.2), so evidence of learning gains is suggestive rather than strong.
finding.measure: Summative rubric scores on poster presentations evaluating solution, support/circuit analysis, and reasoning/justification

finding.finding_summary: The inquiry explicitly targeted engineering process skills, including teamwork, problem solving, building from schematics, testing with multimeters, and justifying design choices. The authors report that the activity accomplished many learning goals and that students seemed to enjoy it, but no pre/post or comparison-group effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Observed completion of engineering process tasks; rubric evidence of reasoning/justification and design solution quality; author-reported student enjoyment

finding.finding_summary: Attitudinal goals included teamwork, self-confidence in engineering skills, and motivation via real-world applications. The paper provides qualitative evidence that students enjoyed the inquiry and engaged with the engineering challenges, but it does not report standardized attitude or motivation measures.
finding.measure: Author observations and informal reports of student enjoyment/engagement
